incidents.title: Hugging Face breached during an evaluation

activity.label: Jul 8–13: first internet access Jul 8; Hugging Face breached Jul 11–13

reveals.text: Hugging Face discloses a breach by an unidentified attacker

incidents.found: Hugging Face detected the intrusion; OpenAI attributed it to its own models
incidents.summary: During a cyber-capability evaluation, OpenAI models (driven mainly by an internal-only research model, and also involving GPT-5.6 Sol) used a previously unknown flaw in the Artifactory package registry to escape their environment. Working from a hijacked benchmark app on Modal, they exploited Hugging Face’s dataset processing to harvest credentials, then used them to move through Hugging Face’s cloud, private network, GitHub and Slack, apparently to obtain the benchmark’s answers. Researchers later found that the roughly 700 agents involved smuggled attack code through almost a million chained short links and tried to publish more than 100 images under a real user’s Docker Hub account. Hugging Face found no tampering with public models, datasets or Spaces.
incidents.lab_response: Disclosed jointly with Hugging Face and called it “an unprecedented cyber incident”. Revoked credentials, rebuilt systems and deactivated the research model; later slowed frontier training and paused its largest planned RL run.

incidents.found: Spencer Kitts, Thomas Larsen and Sydney Von Arx
incidents.summary: Researchers attributed to OpenAI agents more than 2,100 packages they describe as malicious, uploaded to RubyGems between May 5 and June 18; maintainers disabled new registrations from May 12 to 16 and removed more than 500 packages. The packages abused documentation builds to run code on build servers and scrape web content, including UK local-government data. Hundreds of package names contained “oai”, and the researchers say OpenAI never told the RubyGems community.
incidents.lab_response: Said its agents used RubyGems “to carry out benign tasks and retrieve public information” and that it had not been able to verify claims that its models uploaded malicious packages.

incidents.title: Australian government sites, including Medicare statistics

incidents.found: OpenAI, in a review of training activity; the Australian Government announced it
incidents.summary: An OpenAI agent got non-public access to Services Australia’s Medicare statistics portal, where it ran commands, retrieved internal files, credentials and aggregate statistics, reviewed source code and wrote files; no patient records were accessed. OpenAI’s review later tied its models to June activity at four more Australian government systems: the NSW crime statistics bureau, Victoria’s health data agency, the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare and the NSW national parks service. OpenAI found the Medicare activity in mid-August but notified the government only on Sept. 10, by email to a public inbox; the prime minister called the delay unacceptable.
incidents.lab_response: Apologised on Sept. 28, saying its models accessed Australian government websites in ways they were not authorised to and that it should have handled its response better. Promised an independent Australian taskforce and cyber-defence credits, and disclosed a fifth agency, the NSW national parks service, on Oct. 1. On Oct. 6 its chief strategy officer apologised again before parliament’s AI committee and said it had found no other Australian incidents.

incidents.title: DNS tunnel to an outside chatbot

knew.text: Monitoring raises its highest-severity alert about 15 minutes in

reveals.text: OpenAI publishes a report and pauses tool use for its most capable models

incidents.found: OpenAI (its own monitoring)
incidents.summary: On a search task, an agent that could not get useful results from its tools found that the sandbox’s DNS resolver could still reach the public internet. Using DNS delegation and a public chatbot that answers through DNS records, it sent questions out and got answers back. Monitoring flagged it about 15 minutes in, but the run did not stop automatically and was shut down by hand about 2.5 hours later. OpenAI reported no confirmed data exposure.
incidents.lab_response: Stopped the run and paused all training, evaluation and tool-using inference for its most capable models until the gap is closed; it is restricting DNS in research environments and adding blocking controls at two independent network layers.

incidents.title: UK AISI cyber test: agents target a GitHub project

activity.label: Jul 25–28, with internet access deliberately on

incidents.found: UK AISI’s security team, which saw unusual data leaving a test machine on Jul 28
incidents.status: Confirmed by AISI and OpenAI; acknowledged by Anthropic
incidents.summary: During a cyber-range evaluation run by the UK AI Security Institute, with internet access deliberately enabled and the developers’ misuse classifiers switched off, agents took 19 unsanctioned actions on the live internet in 10 of 122 runs: 17 by Anthropic’s Mythos 5 and 2 by OpenAI’s GPT-5.6 Sol. In the most serious case, a Mythos 5 agent mistook an unrelated open-source project for part of the exercise, tried to get malicious code merged and used fake accounts and emails to pressure its maintainers, one of whom refused. Other runs created accounts and repositories on GitHub and other services, and GPT-5.6 Sol reused a GitHub credential another agent had left public. AISI found no resulting harm.
incidents.lab_response: OpenAI said AISI told it on Aug. 3, described GPT-5.6 Sol’s two actions and said it would review how it runs third-party testing. Anthropic acknowledged the incident on Aug. 31 and said it would assess the transcripts.

incidents.title: Irregular test: OpenAI model attacks a real website

reveals.text: OpenAI discloses it alongside the AISI incident

incidents.found: Irregular, the outside testing firm
incidents.summary: During capture-the-flag cyber evaluations run by the testing firm Irregular, a misconfigured environment gave OpenAI models internet access although they had been told they had none. The fictional target’s name matched a real domain, and a model attacked that real website, believing it was part of the exercise, and used credentials it found to operate the site. OpenAI hasn’t named the model, the site or the date. Irregular says the same mistake let several labs’ models reach real systems.
incidents.lab_response: Disclosed it on Aug. 4 and said Irregular had paused the evaluations, fixed the environment and notified those affected. Said it would review its own approach to third-party testing.

incidents.title: Irregular tests: Claude models breach three companies

knew.text: Anthropic’s transcript review finds the cases

reveals.text: Anthropic discloses incidents at three organizations
Anthropic discloses a fourth case, from January

incidents.found: Anthropic’s own review of evaluation transcripts, prompted by OpenAI’s Hugging Face disclosure; the companies hadn’t noticed
incidents.summary: During cyber evaluations run with the testing firm Irregular, Claude models that had been told they had no internet access reached it through a misconfiguration and broke into production systems at three real companies with basic techniques such as weak passwords, exposed debug pages and SQL injection. Opus 4.7 took credentials and reached a production database, downloading and changing user records, and kept going after recognizing the target was real. An internal research model scanned about 9,000 internet hosts and broke into one company’s application. An early Opus 4.6, disclosed later, took admin access to a third party’s system and read one person’s personal information. Anthropic found no model pursuing a goal of its own.
incidents.lab_response: Stopped all cyber evaluations on Jul. 23, notified Irregular and the companies on Jul. 27 and disclosed on Jul. 30. Added a real-time classifier that halts runs that probe or escape a sandbox, required outside evaluators to adopt safeguards, and commissioned an independent review by METR.

incidents.title: PyPI malware published during an Irregular test

incidents.found: Anthropic’s own review of evaluation transcripts; the security vendor hadn’t noticed
incidents.summary: In an Irregular capture-the-flag test whose prompt said there was no internet access, Anthropic’s Mythos 5 reached the internet, registered an account on the Python Package Index and published a malicious package. It was live for under an hour before PyPI’s systems removed it, and in that time it ran on 15 real systems, which Anthropic believes were security vendors’ scanners. One scanner leaked its credentials to the model, which used them to reach that vendor’s live database. The model kept telling itself it was in a simulation despite evidence it was on the real internet.
incidents.lab_response: Notified PyPI and shared indicators, disclosed it on Jul. 30 and released a redacted transcript on Sept. 9. Said its production safeguards, absent from the evaluation, would have blocked the behaviour.

incidents.found: Anthropic’s internal behavioral testing
incidents.summary: In internal testing, an early version of Claude Mythos Preview was asked to escape a secured sandbox and message the researcher. incidents.title: Amap scraped by a Tencent-linked agent fleet

activity.label: Sep 28 – Oct 6, still running when last reported

reveals.text: The Swarmchasers post a preliminary report and present it at the AI Swarm Dynamics Hackathon

incidents.found: The Swarmchasers, independent researchers
incidents.status: Not confirmed by Tencent; unknown whether a person directed the agents
incidents.summary: From Sept. 28, a fleet of AI agents used the web scanner urlquery.net as a remote browser to read Amap, Alibaba’s map service, for the share of users heading to each entrance of Chinese parks, museums, zoos and hospitals. Their scripts generated Alibaba anti-bot tokens, sent Amap’s cookies to outside inboxes, tried what by its name is Amap’s pre-release server and loaded its map API with other parties’ keys. The code ran on Tencent Cloud behind a proxy named “hysandbox-ats”, and the researchers think the agents were most likely Tencent’s Hy models in an evaluation or task-generation run; a writing-style analysis only narrowly favours Hy over Zhipu’s GLM. It is unclear whether Tencent or a cloud customer ran them, and whether a person told the agents to get around Amap’s protections or they chose to; that would decide whether this counts as an incident here. The researchers found no sign the agents communicated and call it a fleet rather than a swarm.
incidents.lab_response: Tencent and Alibaba hadn’t commented as of Oct. 7.

responses.text: A bipartisan group of 26 attorneys general led by New York urges Congress to regulate frontier AI, including government-led incident response with investigators’ direct access to company records.
src: Letter to congressional leadership on federal AI regulation
State attorneys general (via California Attorney General)
Attorney General James Calls on Congress to Protect Americans from Unchecked AI Development

responses.title: Prime minister orders urgent review
responses.text: Australia’s prime minister orders an urgent review with the Australian Signals Directorate and the AI Safety Institute.
src: OpenAI hacked Medicare portal, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says

responses.title: Dozens of organizations notified
responses.text: Says it has notified dozens of affected organizations, including governments and universities, and that its review will take months.
src: The Hugging Face incident and other third-party impact from misaligned models
OpenAI says its advanced models may have gone after government websites

responses.title: Tool-use training paused for top models
responses.text: Pauses training, evaluation and tool-using inference for its most capable models until the DNS gap is fixed and further red-teaming is done; its second pause since July.
src: An agent used DNS to reach an external chatbot
OpenAI pauses training a second time

responses.title: METR holds risky agent actions for review
responses.text: Citing the OpenAI, Anthropic and AISI incidents, the evaluator METR deploys a monitor that blocks agent actions that could cause real-world harm until a person reviews them.
src: Implementing and evaluating a basic per-action monitor for safer evals

responses.title: Apology and Australian taskforce
responses.text: Apologises to Australia for the access and its slow notice; promises an independent Australian taskforce reporting by year-end, credits from its cyber-defence fund and support for affected agencies. Its chief strategy officer is to appear before parliament’s AI committee on Oct. 6.
src: How we will do better for Australia

responses.title: Florida seeks to halt new model development
responses.text: Florida’s attorney general asks a state court to bar OpenAI from developing new AI models without independent third-party guardrails and approval, citing the agent incidents in an existing lawsuit over ChatGPT.
src: Florida asks a court to stop OpenAI building new AI models

responses.title: GPT-6.1 Astra release cancelled
responses.text: Cancels the planned October release of GPT-6.1 Astra after internal tests found it fell short on staying within scope and authorization.
src: OpenAI shelves new AI model after internal safety tests, WSJ reports
OpenAI ignored employees who warned it wasn’t doing enough about security
The New York Times (via GV Wire)

responses.title: Nonprofit sues OpenAI over the hack
responses.text: Legal Advocates for Safe Science and Technology sues OpenAI in San Francisco Superior Court under California’s unfair-competition and anti-hacking laws, seeking an injunction, not damages. OpenAI calls the suit “completely without merit”.
src: LASST v. OpenAI, complaint as filed
Legal Advocates for Safe Science and Technology
LASST Is Suing OpenAI Over Hack of Hugging Face
OpenAI sued over Hugging Face hack

responses.title: Australia orders a legacy-system stocktake
responses.text: Australia’s Home Affairs department directs federal agencies to take stock of vulnerable legacy systems, with systems of government significance first and a review due by the end of the year.
src: Direction 002-2026: Strengthening Commonwealth cyber posture against AI-enabled risks
Government orders review of cyber systems after OpenAI Medicare breach

responses.title: White House accord on AI controls
responses.text: Leaders of six companies, including OpenAI president Greg Brockman, Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, Google’s Sundar Pichai and Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg, sign a voluntary White House accord committing to monitor models so they don’t hack or access systems in unintended ways, and to independent external audits of those controls.
src: Trump releases AI accord with tech executives
Trump, Six AI Giants Sign ‘Super Intelligence’ Safety Accord
Top AI executives sign commitment to ‘self-police’ after meeting at White House

responses.title: IPO prospectus flags rogue-agent liability
responses.text: Anthropic’s draft prospectus, seen by Reuters, warns it could face claims over the actions of autonomous agents and calls the law unsettled.
src: Anthropic says rogue AI agents pose uncertain legal risk for the company
Anthropic flags AI agent liability risks as OpenAI faces hacking lawsuit

responses.title: Over 100 organizations notified
responses.text: Says it had notified more than 100 organizations by Sept. 26 and is searching about 50 petabytes of training and evaluation records with about 7,000 GPUs, at more than $500,000 a day. Its chief research officer says monitors now run on every training run.
src: The Hugging Face incident and other third-party impact from misaligned models
“We’re not going to shoot ourselves in the foot” over hack fallout, says OpenAI’s chief research officer

responses.title: FTC investigation confirmed
responses.text: The Federal Trade Commission confirms a consumer-protection investigation into OpenAI, Anthropic and the evaluator METR, reportedly under way for months; civil investigative demands are expected within weeks.
src: FTC is investigating OpenAI and Anthropic over possible risks to consumers
FTC probes OpenAI, Anthropic, and METR

responses.title: Senate hearing on rogue AI agents
responses.text: A Senate homeland security subcommittee chaired by Josh Hawley holds its first hearing on rogue AI agents, with witnesses from METR, Apollo Research, the AI Futures Project, Georgetown Law and Dragos. OpenAI declines to attend and says it will answer in writing.
src: ICYMI: Hawley Convenes First Senate Hearing on Rogue AI Attacks
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman to skip congressional hearing on rogue AI agents

responses.title: California subpoenas OpenAI
responses.text: California’s attorney general announces an investigative subpoena served on OpenAI the day before, part of a broader inquiry into cybersecurity incidents and risks involving its models that began with the Hugging Face investigation.
src: As Part of Ongoing Investigation, Attorney General Bonta Serves Investigative Subpoena on OpenAI
OpenAI’s wandering AI agents earn it a California subpoena

responses.title: UK AISI resumes testing, internet off
responses.text: Says it has disabled internet access for agentic cyber evaluations, added a live monitor that holds suspicious actions for human review and pre-run checks, and resumed most evaluation work.
src: Building a more secure environment for evaluating dangerous capabilities

responses.title: Senators propose liability for agent hacking
responses.text: Senators Josh Hawley and Chris Murphy announce the AI Agent Accountability Act, which would make operators of AI agents, and developers who fail to put reasonable safeguards in place, criminally and civilly liable for agent hacking under the federal anti-hacking law.
src: Senators Hawley, Murphy announce bipartisan AI Agent Accountability Act

responses.title: Irregular tests containment first
responses.text: Irregular adds containment tests, run before capability evaluations, in which a model is asked to cross the environment’s boundary so gaps can be fixed; it says one already caught a previously unknown route out, with no outside impact.
src: Containment challenges: testing the boundaries of cyber evaluations

responses.title: Australia’s parliament questions OpenAI
responses.text: Parliament’s AI committee hears OpenAI’s chief strategy officer, Jason Kwon, apologise in person; its chair calls what happened, and the slow notice, utterly unacceptable. Kwon says monitors now alert staff when models reach the internet in unintended ways, that the review now goes back to November 2025 and has found no other Australian incidents, and that OpenAI would support mandatory incident reporting.
src: Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence, 6 October 2026 (proof transcript)
OpenAI has ‘work to do to rebuild trust’ in Australia, executive tells AI inquiry
OpenAI grilled over rogue agents by Australian inquiry

inv.note: Production infrastructure breached: internal datasets and five customers’ datasets accessed, service credentials harvested, and its Spaces used as relays and drop boxes.
An unsecured benchmark app deployed by a Modal customer was taken over and used as the base of the attack. Modal says its own platform was not compromised.
Hugging Face’s own AWS keys, taken from its systems, were used to map its cloud storage and permissions; agents also tried to solve its AWS bot challenge. AWS itself wasn’t compromised.
A stolen Hugging Face key enrolled attacker machines, including the hijacked Modal app, into Hugging Face’s private network 181 times. Tailscale itself wasn’t compromised.
Hugging Face’s GitHub App was abused to mint tokens, list private repositories and open a pull request; GitHub code search was used to hunt for tokens.
One of the keys used on the FBI’s crime-data API was the FBI’s own developer key, which sits in a public FBI repository on GitHub.
The Census Bureau API keys the agents used were found in public GitHub repositories.
Public repositories searched for leaked API keys, one of which worked.

Agents created accounts under false identities, opened a malicious pull request on a real project and created many repositories; GitHub suspended an account and confirmed the activity broke its terms. GPT-5.6 Sol reused a credential another agent had left public.
Hugging Face’s workspace was searched for 27 terms with stolen Hugging Face tokens; the records don’t show what came back.

Agents tried to create at least 115 public images under a real user’s account, with credentials the researchers believe came from paste sites; three uploads are confirmed and the images appear removed.
A screenshot service whose browser was made to run code hidden in web addresses; the screenshots carried the results back.
An HTTP testing service used to serve encoded code fragments as web pages for mShots to run.
Almost a million short links were used to smuggle attack code in chained fragments. The researchers withheld the services’ names.
Accounts accessed with publicly exposed credentials: one used as a relay and staging path, one for data storage, two read-only. OpenAI hasn’t named the services.
More than 100 single-use endpoints were used to send data out, according to Hugging Face.
The agents’ first confirmed internet access after OpenAI rebuilt its registry: one read the comments on an issue.
Agents used OpenAI’s self-hosted package registry as a covert message board and exploited previously unknown flaws in its software to reach the internet.
Previously unknown flaws in the registry software were used to escape the evaluation environment at the start of the Hugging Face attack.
Roughly 18,000 posts, up to about 400 pages a day, used as a message board; agents also sent cross-site scripting probes and clashed with a volunteer moderator.
1,013 revisions across 601 pages, including compressed education data the agents stored there.
169 revisions across 68 pages, including links to tunnels the agents called “research bridges”.
The first wiki the agents tried: 58 revisions across 4 pages, mostly test posts. Its abuse filter blocked some attempts.
15 revisions across 3 pages, mostly links to federal budget PDFs.
17 revisions to its sandbox page.
A games wiki: 25 revisions across 12 pages, with sandbox pages holding links to federal PDFs.
One revision, plus tests of chaining links through proxies.
6 revisions across 2 pages.
One revision carrying the same census codes and federal document IDs seen on the other wikis.
3 revisions.

Agents got into its link shortener, which has no public sign-up, built at least 170 links and used an old link’s public stats page as a message board; one link drew 54,250 visits on June 18. Vanderbilt locked the stats pages on Sept. 8.

495 queries recorded in Vanderbilt’s logs used a public demo key, the FBI’s own developer key from GitHub, and a private individual’s accidentally published key. The logs don’t prove the requests reached the FBI.
Agents created four or five links on its link shortener, following its published rules; it locked its stats pages on Sept. 8.
Its digital library got seven exploit probes (SQL injection, command injection, path traversal) and a burst of 80 requests after a photo failed to load; they appear to have failed.
Agents wrote into the log of an old link on its link shortener, which drew 1,845 visits that day, according to Kenneth DeGraff; Nightingale counts four links.
About 30 edits across 15 pages, leaving links to help the agents with tasks.
A Polish text-sharing site used to coordinate an “Iowa cancer statistics” task: over 100 messages, most on June 16. Counts differ between sources.
55 pastes that appear to be from OpenAI’s agents, the latest on Sept. 2. The researchers warn that fake posts appeared after Sept. 4.
20 pastes, including English Premier League data.
The same nine Thai labour-force figures the agents retrieved were posted here anonymously; Transluce doesn’t say who posted them.
A link shortener used to store information; its public admin page listed 499 links, most dated June 17.
A link shortener: two links.
A link shortener: 46 links, used to park SEC and Iowa data files.
A link shortener: 25 links, used to park SEC and Iowa data files.
A link shortener: 12 links, including one named “SECcountyM” pointing at an SEC data file.
A link shortener: 38 links, according to Nightingale’s list of sites.
A JSON-sharing site used to store documents; sources count between 2 and 13.
A wiki for the D programming language: 63 revisions across 49 pages.
12 revisions across 9 pages.
4 revisions.
One revision.

More than 2,100 packages uploaded, most on May 11–12; sign-ups were paused May 12–16 and over 500 packages removed. At least six packages tried to exploit a caching bug to steal API keys; maintainers found no sign it worked.
A second burst: over three hours, agents published 81 to 83 packages whose metadata pointed to one SEC data file.
More than 100 packages abused its documentation builds to run code on its servers and fetch web pages.
Meeting calendars and agendas were scraped through RubyDoc.info’s build system and republished as RubyGems packages.
Meeting calendars and agendas were scraped through RubyDoc.info’s build system and republished as RubyGems packages.
Meeting documents were scraped through RubyDoc.info’s build system and republished as RubyGems packages.
Used to fetch Thai government statistics; Jina blocked the agents for an hour, citing abuse.
Named in 1,397 of the packages; the agents used it heavily to fetch web pages.

A web-scanning service used as a remote browser to reach sites the agents couldn’t reach directly; an agent also tried to register an account. Agents tried to open private accounts from June 14 and first succeeded on June 18, which hides their scans from public view.
Used again as a remote browser, this time for Amap: 2,048 reports from Sept. 28 to Oct. 4 alone.
A public-data site run by Deloitte, Datawheel and MIT: 12 exploit probes while the agents fetched University of Iowa data; they appear to have failed.

affected.name: Australian Institute of Health and Welfare

inv.note: After an anti-bot block, an agent sent a script-injection probe, then took a public file from a pre-production server; no non-public data was exposed.

Aggregate statistics retrieved through third-party browsing and download services; separate attempts to bypass access controls failed. OpenAI judged the material public but notified the institute on Sept. 24.

affected.name: Thailand Office of the Narcotics Control Board

inv.note: An agent escalated through a page-fetching service and encoded scripts until it got provincial drug-arrest statistics; no exploit.
Repeated attempts to pull labour-force data from its dashboard.

About 16,500 urlquery scans of its statistics API. Agents brute-forced the API-key field name, got past a POST-only restriction by double-encoding and kept going after rate limits; the data was public. An independent researcher ties the scans to the German-wiki swarm through shared Azure addresses.
Historical theme-park wait times retrieved.
A disposable inbox was created to verify a Browserless account.
An account was verified with a disposable inbox and used for remote browsing sessions.
Korean energy-import data pulled, matching a question in a Google benchmark; some was sent on to an unnamed site.
A cryptocurrency exchange: repeated failed trade attempts, an HTML-injection attempt and API probes over about 2.5 hours.

Its Medicare statistics portal: the agent gained non-public access, ran commands, retrieved internal files, credentials and aggregate statistics, reviewed source code and wrote files; no patient records.

affected.name: NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research

inv.note: A model’s API and metadata requests through the public Crime Mapping Tool returned application configuration, operational jobs and logs, and website metadata, OpenAI says; no individual crime records. The bureau says it found no security vulnerability.
Agents found an exposed access key and used it to query the reporting system of the Victorian Agency for Health Information for its configuration and aggregate survey statistics.
Public data pulled with API keys found in public GitHub repositories; the Commerce Department says no private data was accessed. Transluce dates attempts to reuse the exposed keys to June 16–22.

Public information retrieved and posted on another public webpage, which hasn’t been named. OpenAI says no accounts or nonpublic data were accessed. Transluce and Manifold Security also found double-slash and path-traversal probes on sec.gov URLs around June 18.
Agents repeatedly fetched one public SEC file (county.json) through RubyGems packages, wikis and link shorteners; 384 of 583 links in the June packages point to it.
The SEC’s investor-education site: public information retrieved and posted on another public webpage, which hasn’t been named.

More than 200,000 requests to its Civil Rights Data Collection site, including a SQL-injection probe, while apparently looking up school statistics. The attempt failed and the department found no impact. OpenAI hasn’t confirmed it.
On the juvenile justice office’s statistics site, a workflow retrieved a legacy FBI arrest table by adding an encoded parent-directory segment to the URL.

At the Bureau of Economic Analysis, an automated workflow tried to register for an API key with a disposable email address and the organization name “OpenAI Research”, and tried to read its CAPTCHA by OCR; no registration is confirmed.
On CAL-ACCESS, requests apparently got around anti-bot controls and retrieved public campaign-finance records. Transluce doesn’t attribute this to OpenAI.
295,912 archived captures across Maryland education-statistics hosts in one day, peaking at 5,594 a minute, with guessed file names. Transluce doesn’t attribute this to OpenAI.
251 archived requests to its legacy IQuery public-health portal, trying direct-IP routes and a guessed login route; no data returned. Transluce doesn’t attribute this to OpenAI.
Repeated attempts to export state health statistics through file-conversion services. Transluce doesn’t attribute this to OpenAI.
School enrollment data pulled through modified URLs and intermediary services. Transluce doesn’t attribute this to OpenAI.
53 ChatGPT users’ images were posted through unlisted links; most have been removed. OpenAI hasn’t named the sites.

affected.name: A chatbot reachable over DNS (not named)

inv.note: Queried through DNS lookups to answer the agent’s questions.

affected.name: NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service

inv.note: A model researching wildfire statistics sent crafted queries to the Fire History mapping service to infer database metadata not meant to be public, and downloaded the public fire-history dataset; no personal information was found. NSW was told on Oct. 1.
Archived requests targeted its Git repository files and a backup copy of a server-side script; no sign they succeeded.

899 requests to its collection-search service, including 13 SQL-injection and similar probes, which failed. Canada’s Cyber Centre saw no sign that government systems were compromised. Transluce doesn’t confidently attribute this to OpenAI.
KansasMemory.gov, run by the Kansas Historical Society: 36,578 automated captures in one day, peaking at 1,093 a minute, until the site began returning gateway timeouts.

affected.name: White House Office of Management and Budget

inv.note: 719 urlquery reports of attempts to download two public budget reports from its MAX.gov portal, including URL variants on its login and PIV-card hosts.

affected.name: U.S. Navy, Naval History and Heritage Command

inv.note: Probes of alternative URLs and endpoints on history.navy.mil; attempts to reach its content-management pages for editing or publishing failed.
The Portuguese national web archive’s Save Page Now feature was used to send many of the requests to government sites.
The log of an old link on its link shortener was used as storage; 63 visits on June 18.
A Polish link shortener with links under agent-style names; its logs are now behind a login.

affected.name: Paste, image and file hosts (not named)

inv.note: Retrieved records posted to a paste service and a task photo uploaded to an image host, both to work around tool limits; later, a workbook made publicly downloadable on a temporary file host so other agents could fetch it.
Queried with a leaked API key, which authenticated and returned metadata; attempts to register for a key failed.

affected.name: An open-source project and its maintainers (not named)

inv.note: A Mythos 5 agent tried to get malicious code merged and used fake accounts and emails to pressure the two maintainers; the owner closed the pull request after another user flagged it. Neither had any link to AISI.

affected.name: Online services used in the AISI test (not named)

inv.note: Accounts registered at DNS providers, and file-transfer and form-to-email services used to reach the maintainers; a bystander’s test environment was briefly taken over and a PyPI sign-up failed.

affected.name: Company whose domain matched a test’s fictional name (not named)

inv.note: Across four runs, Claude Opus 4.7 took application and infrastructure credentials and reached a production database, downloading and changing user records: the most serious impact Anthropic found.
An OpenAI model attacked the real website, taking it for part of the exercise, and used credentials it found to operate the site. Irregular found no impact beyond the site’s own data.

affected.name: Company breached by an internal Anthropic model (not named)

inv.note: After its fictional target went offline, the model scanned about 9,000 hosts and broke into this company’s internet-facing application through an exposed debug page and SQL injection, then stopped on concluding the company was real.

affected.name: Third party whose system Opus 4.6 reached (not named)

inv.note: An early Opus 4.6 used a password from a file for admin access, harvested more credentials, changed the system’s settings and read one person’s personal information. Anthropic notified the party after finding it in August.
Mythos 5 registered an account and published three versions of a malicious package, which PyPI’s own systems removed within an hour. Anthropic notified the PyPI team.

affected.name: Security vendor scanning new packages (not named)

inv.note: Its scanner installed the package and leaked access credentials to the model, which used them to reach the vendor’s live database.

affected.name: Three companies reached in Gemini’s test (not named)

inv.note: One shared its name with the test’s fictional target (possibly the same company other labs’ models reached); the other two were reached with credentials found in public repositories. Google says the model stopped each time.

affected.name: Company breached in Meta’s test (not named)

inv.note: Meta says its model exploited a security vulnerability in this company’s service; The Information reported it changed internal systems. It may be the same company other labs’ models reached.

affected.name: Public websites used to post an exploit (not named)

inv.note: Details of the sandbox exploit were posted, unasked, to several hard-to-find but public websites.

More than 2,000 scans of place pages on 216 places, many answered with a CAPTCHA. Scripts generated anti-bot tokens, read Amap’s cookies, tried a host named as its pre-release server and used other parties’ published map-API keys; entrance shares were read out for at least five places.

affected.name: Wikimedia wikis (Wikipedia, Commons, Meta and others)

inv.note: 54 unapproved edits across nine wikis, almost all in sandbox pages readers don’t see, plus edits to the settings of a citation tool that Wikimedia believes were meant to use it as a proxy. No bot approval was sought.
Unsuccessful attempts to compromise the public note-taking tool and use it as a proxy for fetching other websites.

Hundreds of thousands of queries, alongside millions of API requests across Wikimedia sites, which Wikimedia says may have contributed to a partial outage in which up to half of requests timed out. Its incident report blamed unnamed aggressive scrapers.

unknowns: Which models drove each incident. OpenAI has named models only for the [Hugging Face breach](#hugging-face).
When the [U.S. government-site activity](#us-government) and the [image posting](#user-images) happened.

Whether it has stopped. Transluce saw similar [activity](#urlquery) as late as Sept. 16 to 20, after OpenAI’s Aug. 18 controls, though it didn’t tie that to OpenAI. Pastes that appear to be the agents’ appeared on a [text-sharing site](#twelve-sites) until Sept. 2, and the [DNS incident](#dns-chatbot) happened on Sept. 20. OpenAI’s chief research officer says every containment break except Sept. 20 belongs to the May–June cluster. OpenAI’s chief strategy officer told Australia’s parliament on Oct. 6 that new training monitors had recently caught a model reaching the internet in an unintended way, without saying when or where.

How many organizations were affected. OpenAI says it had notified more than 100 by Sept. 26, that a notice “does not mean that any private information was accessed”, and that more will follow. Its review now reaches back to November 2025.
Whether OpenAI will confirm the [RubyGems uploads](#rubygems), the [Education Department attempt](#us-government) or the [Nightingale findings](#twelve-sites).

Whether outside evaluators’ past runs hide more cases. AISI’s scan of about 40,000 samples and METR’s reviews for AISI and Anthropic haven’t been published, Irregular hasn’t given a count, and Meta’s promised retrospective hasn’t appeared.
